meta.title: Who really said "The robbed that smiles, steals something from the thief"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — it's genuine Shakespeare. The Duke of Venice speaks it in Othello, Act 1, Scene 3 (c.1603–04). Verified against the Folger and MIT texts.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The robbed that smiles, steals something from the thief'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Shakespeare: the Duke of Venice, Othello Act 1 Scene 3. The modern spelling of 'The robb'd that smiles...' Verified against Folger & MIT texts.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Shakespeare’s. The line is spoken by the Duke of Venice in ‘Othello’, Act 1, Scene 3, consoling Brabantio — confirmed against the Folger and MIT texts. The popular form is just the modern spelling of the original “The robb’d that smiles…”

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt:
The robb’d that smiles, steals something from the thief;
He robs himself that spends a bootless grief.
trail: Confirmed verbatim in the Folger Shakespeare Library text of Othello, Act 1, Scene 3, in the Duke of Venice’s speech.
Independently confirmed against the MIT Shakespeare edition, which shows the same couplet ending “…spends a bootless grief.”
The line is part of a set of rhymed “sentences” the Duke offers Brabantio, who feels robbed of his daughter Desdemona by Othello.
source.excerptNote: The popular one-line quotation is the first half of this rhymed couplet, given modern spelling (“robbed” for “robb’d”). “Bootless” means futile or useless.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: About William Shakespeare
author.bio: William Shakespeare was an English playwright, poet and actor, widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language. Othello, his tragedy of jealousy and manipulation, was written around 1603–04 and first printed in a 1622 quarto and the 1623 First Folio. This line belongs not to Othello himself but to the Duke of Venice, who offers it as consolation early in the play.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The author here is genuine — this really is Shakespeare. The common slips are about who in the play says it, and about the quotation being trimmed.

items.why: Many quote sites label the line “Shakespeare, Othello” in a way that implies Othello himself speaks it. In fact it is the Duke of Venice, consoling Brabantio in Act 1, Scene 3 — well before Othello’s own tragedy unfolds.

The popular quotation stops at “…steals something from the thief,” but Shakespeare wrote it as a rhymed couplet: “He robs himself that spends a bootless grief.” The modern spelling “robbed” also replaces the original elided “robb’d.”

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution to Shakespeare is correct — the line is the Duke of Venice’s in Othello, Act 1, Scene 3, quoted in modern spelling and usually shorn of its second line.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In the scene, Brabantio has just lost the fight to keep his daughter Desdemona from Othello. The Duke, unable to reverse the marriage, offers a string of consoling maxims — and this couplet is one of them: a victim who meets loss with a smile denies the thief the pleasure of his grief, while endless mourning only robs the mourner further.

Brabantio, unpersuaded, retorts that such tidy sayings are cold comfort — “these sentences… are equivocal” — which is part of why the line reads as proverbial wisdom lifted cleanly out of its dramatic context.
